articles.title: European Defense Strategy Confronts Lethal Dependency on American Constellations
articles.content: Recent days have made clear the folly of relying too much for your national security on a capricious private citizen named Elon Musk. Mr Musk is said to have ordered the partial hobbling of his satellite-internet service inside Ukraine. That had two malign effects. It hampered Ukraine’s already limited ability to defend its cities and civilians from fast and deadly Russian drones. It also made it harder for Ukraine to strike back at Russia’s occupying forces. If President Donald Trump objected to this egregious favour to the Kremlin, he kept quiet about it. America’s allies, in Europe and elsewhere, may reasonably ask how much they can trust the superpower. If, in the future, they need space-based communications systems to defend themselves against attack, can they be absolutely certain that America will supply them unconditionally? The problem, alas, is that no adequate home-grown alternative exists. Europe talks a good game of trying to achieve „autonomy in space”. But that will take time and money, and also require Europe to cut the waste, infighting and duplication that have weighed down its space efforts. How to get there? First, Europe must have the launch capacity to put large numbers of satellites into orbit. In this, its record so far is poor. It can lift heavy payloads into space on its Ariane rockets, but nowhere near as cheaply or efficiently as Mr Musk’s company does. Europe’s rocket programme exemplifies flaws of its space ventures. Delays in developing its heavy-lift launcher, the Ariane 6, left Europe without access to space for almost a year in 2023 and 2024. The European Space Agency (ESA), which funds the programme, is partly to blame. It fails to award contracts to the most innovative or efficient suppliers, instead favouring firms from countries that donate the most funds. The programme is also shielded from market forces, getting roughly €300m ($337m) a year in public subsidies. Small wonder it has been trounced by SpaceX, which last year launched Falcon 9 rockets 165 times, charging private clients $70m a pop, while Ariane charges more than $90m despite those subsidies. To fix this, the ESA is tentatively copying America’s space agency, NASA, which decades ago encouraged the growth of commercial space firms by switching from „cost-plus” contracts for developing rockets to buying fixed-price launch services, a policy that let Mr Musk’s SpaceX flourish. The agency has awarded contracts to three rocket startups. Mergers, such as the proposed tie-up of three of Europe’s biggest satellite-making businesses, could follow. But can Europe create a firm big enough to compete globally without reducing competition at home? Europe’s second priority should be to create a rival to Mr Musk’s Starlink, and to do so without policies that drive up prices and stifle innovation. OneWeb, a firm part-owned by the British and French governments, already provides some services similar to Starlink’s. The European Union is going ahead with IRIS2, a €16bn project to deploy 348 satellites to provide secure communications to governments and armed forces. Yet even this suffers from fragmentation and duplication. Germany plans to build a swarm of 100 military-communications satellites at a cost of about €10bn, while France and Britain are investing in their own smaller programmes. It would be wiser for all to pool their demand for satellite services. Some governments will insist on having such systems under national control. Yet their concerns could be met by building satellites to common standards, so that they are interoperable. Countries or blocs could own these, but by linking them together, all would benefit: larger fleets would mean more resilience and greater coverage. Examples of this are already in orbit, such as small radar satellites built by Iceye, a Finnish firm. It offers customers a „federated model”, in which they can choose how much to share intelligence and co-ordinate where their satellites focus. Such an approach should encourage like-minded middle powers beyond Europe, such as Canada, Japan and South Korea, to co-operate too. Europe need not stop there. The more it builds up its own space capabilities and shares them with America, the more convincingly it can show that an alliance of democracies is valuable. If so, despite Mr Trump’s instincts, America would have much to lose by holding its allies to ransom. © 2026 The Economist Newspaper Limited. All rights reserved. articles.title: Amazon Labor Surveillance Testifies Before European Parliament Lawmakers
articles.content: The European Parliament’s employment committee has highlighted the need for regulating automated control of workers after visiting Amazon warehouses in Germany and Poland this week. Seven of the committee MEPs visited Amazon warehouses employing some 5,000 workers on Monday and Tuesday (26-27 October) ahead of the Commission’s Quality Jobs Act proposal expected in December. The trip follows the committee’s hearing on working conditions in Amazon in January, where workers raised concerns about efficiency goals, safety, and surveillance using AI tools, which may be regulated more rigorously as a part of the upcoming act. According to a 2023 survey by UNI Europa, a labour union federation, about a half of Amazon’s employees said their work had a negative impact on their mental and physical health. Workers’ progress throughout the day is usually watched through security cameras, but also the work badges scanned in check points in various locations in the warehouse, and scanning devices used to identify products.  In the city of Sosnowiec, home to one of Amazon’s Polish warehouses, employees are overworked by “constant pressure of being judged, which is very hard to cope with mentally,” Agata Wypiór, recently-named vice secretary of Amazon’s European Works Council and Solidarność union leader told EUobserver. Leaving worker management and performance monitoring to algorithms means “these processes become almost invisible,” Li Andersson, head of the delegation, told EUobserver. “The way the workers describe it, it sounds like a digital panopticon: when you work faster you have to work even faster.“  Workers themselves often do not know what data is collected on them and how it is being used to set productivity targets, Anderssen highlighted.  To read this story, log in or subscribe Enjoy access to all articles and 25 years of archives, comment and gift articles. articles.title: Anthropic Public Benefit Governance Threatens Multi-Billion Dollar Institutional Valuation
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAnthropic is aiming to go public as a public benefit corporation, a rare structure for publicly traded companies.It will require by law Anthropic to balance a mandate for public benefit with standard fiduciary responsibilities.Analysts and experts say it could have a long-term impact on valuation of the hot AI company, and come into play during merger and acquistion activity.Anthropic's logo is displayed on a smartphone, with a page from the company's website about its IPO filing in the background, in Creteil, France, on October 27, 2026. Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAnthropic's structure as a public benefit corporation (PBC) raises critical questions for investors ahead of the AI lab's blockbuster IPO. Anthropic aims to go public at a valuation of $1.5 trillion or more, making it the first major frontier lab to test public markets' appetite for AI – at a potentially rich valuation. The PBC wrapper adds another wrinkle, requiring Anthropic to balance a mandate for public benefit with standard fiduciary responsibilities as a publicly traded corporation. Anthropic's goal, according to its S-1 filing, is "to responsibly develop and maintain advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." Other companies operate as PBCs or under similar structures. Warby Parker is a PBC. Privately held Patagonia is registered as similar Benefit Corp. in California. When Google went public in 2004, its informal motto was "don't be evil," which it included in its IPO prospectus and corporate code of conduct, though Google is not a PBC. Anthropic has long pitched itself as the responsible AI firm and has taken measures to police its own conduct. In 2023, Anthropic set up a "long-term benefit trust" to oversee its business practices. The company also established a "public benefit fund" with about 847 million shares of Class N stock, or roughly 5% of its fully diluted shares as of June 30. Seven co-founders, including Dario Amodei, have special voting power through a single Class F share equal to 50.1% of total voting power over matters brought to a shareholder vote. Anthropic said in its filing that it believes those seven are "distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission." Anthropic gave itself a long leash to act as it sees fit. Operating as a PBC "gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose that we promote," the company said in its S-1. Legal experts say that Anthropic's PBC structure could create tension in how it operates. "The obligation of directors is to balance achievement of [public] purpose with achievement of profit, and if you ask me what that means – 'to balance' – I would say, 'Good luck,'" said Lawrence Hamermesh, a Delaware corporate law attorney with decades of experience in PBC law. PBC law is ambiguous on a key word, "balance," he adds, pointing out that there's no fundamental criterion to distinguish when one interest takes precedence over the other. "It's hard enough in the ordinary case to win a damages claim against directors for having screwed up and having cost the company some money," he said. "It's doubly hard to do so in a public benefit corporation where you also have this defense that, 'Hey, I was doing it to promote our stated public benefit.'" How Anthropic handles AI safety is a key risk. Anthropic has been at the forefront in sounding alarms about rapidly advancing AI, outlining legions of risks in its S-1. The company has restricted access to some models it deems too dangerous to be released widely in public. That practice could continue, even if it comes at a cost to revenue and profit growth. Anthropic will also have to balance its PBC mandates with shareholder interests as it continues to raise capital. The company has multiple share classes with varying degrees of control, shareholder, and voting rights. Investors typically charge more for capital in situations that dilute their control from one-share/one vote, points out John Coates, professor of law and economics at Harvard Law School. "If the company needs to continue to raise capital over the foreseeable future, as seems to be true of Anthropic, the company will know they need to pay attention to investors' interests for much of that future," he said in an email to CNBC. The PBC structure "adds another dimension of uncertainty about how this investment may play out." Analysts say investors shouldn't gloss over the PBC structure. "It's interesting to read it right up front in an S-1," Gil Luria, head of technology research at DA Davidson, said. "There's a quote about [how the] goal is for the stock not to trade at higher than the value of the company. Then they talk about things that they do that are not profit-maximizing, like promising never to have ads in Claude … So they led with this, and it's important." Evercore ISI analyst Mark Mahaney said in a Monday note that Anthropic's PBC status will also limit shareholders' power over the operations of the company. "Governance limits shareholder influence: as a public benefit corporation, the board must weigh its mission alongside returns, an independent trust elects a majority of directors, and the co-founders hold 50.1% of the vote," he said. Granted, Anthropic could alter or scrap its PBC status, and there's precedent for doing so. Shoe-maker-turned-AI-company Allbirds, for instance, dropped its PBC designation as part of a restructuring in June. The industrial structure of the AI sector is not settled, moreover, so investors should be prepared for further changes as the technology progresses. Large-scale mergers and innovative public-private partnerships have been floated by some of the industry's top executives, and U.S. authorities are considering ways to audit the technology and implement development standards. "We are dealing with this issue today," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC last week. "This is an issue of the moment."

articles.title: GitHub Deploys Four Million Cores Against Outage Crisis
articles.content: Re-architects site to cope with AI slop-pocalypse Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published wed 28 Oct 2026 // 16:30 UTC Make us preferred on Google How Google fumbled the frontend with Angular 2 10 hours ago Microsoft faces potential vote: Shareholders curious about its plans to tackle emissions 11 hours ago Take it on the chin SatNad: Microsoft chief exec's pay slips 6% in record year 1 day ago Microsoft releases out-of-band Windows fixes with certificate updates 1 day ago UK ministers had plenty of time for AI datacenter bosses, but none for environmental groups 1 day ago GitHub's Universe conference kicked off in San Francisco on Wednesday with news that its infrastructural universe is expanding to address staggering demand from AI agents. GitHub recorded 7.4 billion code commits in September 2026, five times more than hit its servers a year earlier. This surge in traffic over the past year, the result of developers running AI agents and generating increased amounts of programming code, caught the company unprepared and led to a series of outages and service availability woes. AI-driven code commits started becoming a problem last December, and led to problems in February , April , August , not to mention the months in between. On May 7, the site's 90-day availability hit a low of about 84 percent , according to reconstructed data from GitHub's status page. GitHub execs apologized and promised to do better. Those commitments have put four million CPU cores and 160 petabytes of high-speed storage on its infrastructure roadmap, alongside extra compute capacity for GitHub Actions, the company's beleaguered continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) platform. The Microsoft-owned code hosting biz also says it is redesigning its technical architecture (an effort discussed previously ) to separate compute and storage, with the expectation that will enable 35x more throughput. "We’re also migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure , while continuing to serve incredible levels of traffic from developers around the world," said Jay Parikh, EVP of CoreAI, Microsoft, in a blog post provided to The Register . "We expect to complete the migration early next year. Those investments give us more room to grow. The next step is building the systems that handle the work." Also at the its Universe event , GitHub announced general availability of Copilot Fusion, the company's model routing service that was previewed under the name HydraFusion . The idea is that allowing GitHub to route requests to different models can improve task-completion rates while reducing token consumption costs. "Different tasks need different models," said Parikh. "Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task." GitHub is making more bells and whistles available through its Copilot app, including Copilot Projects, for coordinating parallel work; Copilot Connectors, for simplifying how Copilot connects to MCP servers; and Copilot Automations, which are reusable agent tasks. And in what appears to be an effort to boost Copilot usage in the workplace, GitHub is extending Copilot access to all GitHub Enterprise users without requiring any additional per-seat purchases. Customer still get billed for the tokens they use. Microsoft's code collab biz is also expanding its suite of AI services for developers with an offering called AI Scans, which checks pull requests for vulnerabilities in languages not addressed by rule-based scanning and in code that's already merged, plus new reachability analysis tools that allow development to focus on issues that are plausibly exploitable. Another new offering is a package firewall that checks enterprise policy settings before fetching npm packages. ® ai microsoft ai and ml github github copilot devops Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Anthropic Engineer Declares Autonomous Models Eliminate Technical Coding Interviews
articles.content: Why give people tests that AI aces?  Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published wed 28 Oct 2026 // 20:22 UTC Make us preferred on Google Anthropic now lets Claude users jump out of plane without parachute 1 day ago Elvis rightsholders sue Anthropic for stealing songs and leaving them in Heartbreak Hotel 1 day ago Humanity can't afford not to spend $800B on AI, Anthropic insists 2 days ago Trumpets blare and skies part as AI hypefest culminates in Anthropic IPO filing 2 days ago Britain bets big on AI to defend against the threats AI is helping create 2 days ago Why ask a human to complete a coding test when they can just use an AI to help them? Anthropic engineering manager Felix Rieseberg says he has stopped using traditional coding interviews for his team. "Being able to quickly define problems and find elegant solutions was a weak but useful predictor for how successful you’d be on my teams," Rieseberg explained in a blog post on Tuesday. "Small coding challenges in real code did tell us something meaningful about candidates." No longer, he says. The coding interview is dead , as far as he's concerned. "There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both," he insisted. "Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests." In a response posted to social media, Jaana Dogan, principal engineer at Google, said much the same. "I’m not doing a ton of coding interviews nowadays but I’d be interested to interview how people use coding agents," she wrote . "That itself gives me more signals about candidates' coding skills." Several months ago, Google reportedly began reevaluating how it conducts coding interviews and what it looks for in candidates. And while it would be surprising if similar conversations haven't already occurred at other large technology companies where AI agents have demonstrated their coding capabilities, the rest of the tech industry appears to be moving more cautiously than the AI enthusiasts. "We are not seeing tech companies abandon skills assessments widely across the industry—at least not yet," said Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at ZipRecruiter, in an email to The Register . "In fact, based on our October 2026 Employer Survey of 1,500 employers, we see the tech industry (Information sector specifically) is actually the most likely to test for skills, with 62.5 percent of employers requiring formal skill tests on initial applications." Coding interviews at Microsoft, and later Google, Amazon, Facebook, and other tech giants, vary, depending on what the hiring organization aims to evaluate. They may probe technical knowledge related to a specific subject, coding ability in a particular language, general problem-solving skills, team-oriented behavior, or other skills. Stripe's software engineer interview process, according to Educative , consists of a phone screening stage, a technical phone interview, and several further on-site interviews. Rieseberg actually worked there and describes how founder Patrick Collison urged new hires to pay attention to things that seemed out of place. "His bet was that newcomers would spot friction and opportunities that old-timers had long stopped noticing," he said. And Rieseberg appears to have absorbed that viewpoint based on his dismissal of experience: "Hunger beats tenure," he said, perhaps unaware that technology companies have gotten into legal trouble for jettisoning costly veteran employees so they can be replaced by hungry, less expensive young professionals. Technical interviews are seldom just about technical mastery. There are after all many other ways that employees can add value to an organization beyond testable computer science skills. And when employees have access to AI models that can answer technical questions better than job candidates, it makes sense to look more closely at the creativity and social skills people bring to the table. "The change at Anthropic might be reflecting a shift away from technical skills towards more human, soft skills," said Bachaud. "As AI becomes fully capable of writing code, tech employers may be pivoting away from rote technical testing and heavily toward human-centric soft skills." She argues that while AI may be able to code well, it can't replace critical thinking. "A staggering 61.5 percent of Information employers now report that 'critical thinking' is a primary skill lacking in today's candidate pool," she said. "I don’t think the coding interview is going to come back," said Rieseberg. "It's easy to get sentimental given how many copies of 'Algorithms and Data Structures' were bought in hopes of unlocking good jobs and a better future — or how the death of the coding interview is another milestone in software engineering reaching a new level of abstraction." At the same time, he's not certain what will replace it. "I’m probably not the only manager trying to figure out how to interview for people who build well with AI," Rieseberg wrote. "I haven't quite gotten there yet — but I’m scanning resumes and portfolios for little prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking. If you have figured out something better, I’d love to hear how." Bachaud sees technical evaluations changing instead of going away, noting that 70 percent of Information sector employers have switched to proctored or in-person skill assessments as a way to deter cheating with AI. "Ultimately, tech companies aren't necessarily testing less, but the way they are testing is changing," she said. "As AI automates a lot of manual and technical components of jobs, work skills may become more universal. That could lead to an increase in job switching and turnover once economic conditions improve. In our recent survey of workers, we found that AI-related work concerns are causing   a quarter of workers to start thinking about their next role . And as assessments and skills are changing, what roles are available to them might look more different than ever before." ® claude code ai coding agents software engineering anthropic ai and ml Make us preferred on Google

articles.content: Add TT as Preferred Source The government is exploring ways to compensate authors and other content providers for materials used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models, but has yet to determine how content should be valued, licensed or paid for. Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Michelle Lin (林楚茵) raised the issue earlier this month during a meeting of the legislature’s Transportation Committee. She asked whether the Ministry of Digital Affairs would provide content free of charge for AI model training following efforts to obtain voluntarily licensed material from Taiwanese book publishers. She also asked whether the ministry was developing a mechanism for AI developers to pay news outlets for the use of their content. Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) said the ministry is collecting four types of training content through its voluntary initiative: works whose copyright protection has expired and that are in the public domain, book descriptions provided by publishers, book preview material and works that authors have voluntarily licensed. The ministry has not sought AI training material from Taiwanese news outlets, he said. “We are aware that several international news media outlets have signed content authorization agreements with large AI firms, and we would work to facilitate such partnerships in Taiwan,” Lin Yi-ching said. “Our ultimate goal is for large AI firms, particularly those based in the US, to pay for the content they use to train their models,” he said, adding that the ministry is considering only public-domain and voluntarily licensed material to avoid delaying Taiwan’s AI development through potentially protracted legal disputes over content use. The ministry began building a corpus of high-quality traditional Chinese content for Taiwan’s sovereign AI models late last year, initially using materials provided by central and local government agencies. On Sept. 15, it announced rules governing the participation of private publishers and e-book platform operators, including provisions for voluntary participation, content authorization and the removal of works by authors who opt out. As of the middle of this month, the corpus had accumulated 3.3 billion tokens — units of text that AI models use to process and learn language. The government is also studying ways to encourage AI developers to pay for training materials, but has not specified how payments would be calculated, how any revenue would be shared or when a mechanism might be introduced. At a separate meeting convened in July by the Taiwan Intellectual Property Office (TIPO), representatives of magazine publishers and broadcast media proposed measures to ensure AI companies pay for the use of their content. The government should establish a licensing platform to allow media companies to register content for AI companies to use in exchange for payment, CommonWealth Magazine legal affairs director Chiu Ai-lun (邱愛倫) said. She also urged AI companies to disclose the content they license and the sources of their training data. Some international AI companies continued to scrape media Web sites even when the owners have explicitly prohibited such activity, Satellite Television Broadcasting Association secretary-general May Chen (陳依玫) said. She also called for a mechanism to connect content owners with AI companies seeking to license their material. TIPO’s draft Copyright Guidelines for Generative Artificial Intelligence (生成式人工智慧著作權指引) could give the impression that obtaining authorization was the only way to use copyrighted material, Taiwan Innovative Software and Services Association vice chairman Chang Jung-kuei (張榮貴) said. Fair-use provisions, which permit the use of copyrighted material without the rights holder’s permission under certain circumstances, should remain available when data sources are lawfully accessed and the AI-generated output does not replace original works in the market, he said. He also proposed exploring corpus-matching or collective licensing mechanisms. Starbucks Taiwan’s decision to charge for drink customization, which had been free, has sparked consumer backlash, highlighting the challenge of raising prices without making customers feel they are losing value, experts said. Since Oct. 12, customers who order drinks with less or no ice and ask to have the volume topped up with milk or other liquid have been charged an additional NT$15. Topping off drinks without ice was previously free, and disgruntled customers posted photos on social media showing that iced drinks ordered without ice were only half full if the extra NT$15 was not paid. articles.title: Google Cloud Revenue Surges While Free Cash Flow Deteriorates
articles.content: Alphabet’s Google Cloud more than doubled its revenue to $30.7 billion in the third quarter, helping to soften some of the more tepid growth from Google Search and YouTube. But for investors, it wasn’t enough. Recommended Video Despite the strong showing from its cloud business, investors sold off and Alphabet’s after-hours stock price dropped more than 11% following the release of its quarterly results. The drop wiped out more than $280 billion in market value. Aptus Capital Advisors head of equity and portfolio manager David Wagner wrote that Google Cloud did what it was supposed to this quarter. “The problem is everything else,” wrote Wagner. Investors are concerned about sluggish growth in Google’s search business, amid fears it might be swallowed up by “AI cannibalizing the franchise,” Wagner wrote. Google Search rose 12% to $63.4 billion, a marked slowdown from 17% growth in the second quarter and 19% in the first. Analysts were expecting the search business to grow 15%. Tech analyst Dan Ives remained characteristically bullish in a first-take note from his Yorkville Ives equity research. “This is the Cloud print we have been waiting for, and in our view it matters more than a lighter Search number the bears will lean on tonight,” wrote Ives. Alphabet reported third-quarter revenue of $127.6 billion, up 25% from $102.3 billion a year earlier, roughly in line with the $127.9 billion analysts were expecting, according to consensus estimates from S&P Global Visible Alpha. Earnings tumbled to $2.12 a share from $2.87. The drop is due to an $8.7 billion paper loss on Alphabet’s equity investments, which trimmed its earnings by 55 cents per share. Meanwhile, operating income rose 30% from a year ago, but dipped slightly to $40.6 billion compared to $40.8 billion last quarter. “We had a strong quarter and are now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate,” said Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai in a statement. “Our deep full stack approach is driving momentum across the business, with Alphabet revenues growing 25% year-over year.” As for capital spending, investors are eagerly awaiting the figure among all the hyperscalers as the sizzling race for AI compute has pressed companies to splash out $2 trillion in two years. Alphabet reported that capex was $51.4 billion in the third quarter, compared to $24 billion a year ago. The company confirmed its full-year capital spending forecast and capex is expected to reach $200 billion in 2026, and then rise to $300 billion in 2027. Chief financial officer Anat Ashkenazi said more details on capex would be forthcoming in the fourth quarter. Independent tech analyst Luke Lango wrote in a note immediately after Alphabet announced its results that investors were dumping stock for the wrong reason, namely that the paper loss reflects Alphabet’s stake in SpaceX. Lango called it “accounting noise,” rather than a core problem with the business. “Alphabet is now funding the AI buildout with shareholders’ money instead of its own cash,” wrote Lango. “That’s what the market is punishing tonight. But make no mistake: this is a ‘how do we pay for it’ problem not a ‘nobody wants it’ problem.” The third quarter results are Alphabet’s first full results since the tech giant announced it raised $84.8 billion in equity in June, including $10 billion from Berkshire Hathaway , to fund an AI buildout. The heavy spending has pushed Alphabet’s free cash flow into negative territory, clocking in at negative $9.1 billion, compared to negative $5.9 billion in the second quarter. Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global, wrote in a note that investors have worried that Google Cloud’s profit margin had peaked last quarter but it widened to 36.2%. articles.title: Hostile Russian Deepfake Campaigns Target Tight Congressional Contests
articles.content: Social media videos believed to be produced with artificial intelligence and linked to Russia are misusing real people’s names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in the final stretch of midterm voting . One of the targets is Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio. The video, which appears to include some AI manipulation , depicts a newscast and includes pictures of Haya Akbik, who interned for Brown several years ago, and other former staff members. It was appalling to Akbik, who told The Associated Press that any claims attributed to her in the clip are “completely made up.” “It’s my name, it’s my reputation, making this allegation, and it’s just completely false,” she said. “And it harms the senator, someone else, in the process. So, it’s just messed up.” The videos demonstrate how foreign adversaries continue to use a familiar playbook to try to influence American voters who are deciding which party controls Congress next year. The threat could be magnified with AI, a powerful tool for fabricating damaging information that can sometimes appear very real. Another target is James Talarico , who is running against Republican Ken Paxton for a Senate seat in Texas. The video, also believed to include some AI manipulation, is framed as a direct-to-camera confessional from a former student of Talarico. “The most powerful people in the world know they can’t beat James Talarico with the truth, so they’re slandering him with AI deepfakes, foreign bots, and conspiracy theories to protect their broken, corrupt political system,” Talarico spokesperson JT Ennis said in a statement. The social media company X has taken down the initial posts that shared the videos and suspended the users for violating the platform’s rules. However, copies could still be found online Tuesday — some with hundreds of shares — demonstrating how difficult it can be to contain disinformation that can proliferate in the final days of an election. The videos resemble clips from a Russian network known as Storm-1516 that targeted former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris and her running mate, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, two years ago. The new ones bear similar hallmarks and are likely products of the same network, according to Clemson University professor and media forensics expert Darren Linvill. He found that the accounts that shared recent material had also shared former content from Storm-1516. The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the past, it has denied interfering in U.S. elections. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has publicly identified some videos as Russian disinformation in past election cycles, also didn’t respond to a request for comment. Hany Farid, a Dartmouth College professor who studies artificial intelligence deepfakes, said his analyses showed that videos targeting Brown and Talarico were likely either generated or manipulated using the technology. He noted the video targeting Brown is a “fairly low-tech fake.” The other one, targeting Talarico, is likely generated by AI and “it is consistent with previous disinformation campaigns released close to Election Day,” Farid said. Akbik said the video featuring her shows the importance of Congress regulating “AI slop on the internet.” “This is so damaging,” she said. —Ali Swenson, Associated Press The early-rate deadline for the World Changing Ideas Awards is Friday, November 13, at 11:59 p.m. PT. articles.title: Apple Prepares Touchscreen MacBooks Overturning Decades of Product Dogma
articles.content: Ever since Windows 8 paved the way for touchscreen laptops, Apple’s been against them. And the company’s leaders haven’t exactly been shy about making their feelings known. “It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you get fatigue,” Steve Jobs said in 2010 . “It’s ergonomically terrible.” In 2018, Craig Federighi, Apple’s senior vice president of software engineering, told Wired , “Lifting your arm up to poke a screen is a pretty fatiguing thing to do,” adding that he didn’t anticipate ever being into the idea. “We make the world’s best touch computer on an iPad,” John Ternus, Apple’s current CEO and former SVP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal in 2021 . “And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven’t really felt a reason to change that.” Now Apple’s reversing course. With the newly unveiled MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display , Apple has done what its executives spent more than a decade arguing against: It has put a touchscreen on a Mac. As for what finally prompted the change, the simplest explanation may be that the company is just getting with the times. Typically when Apple enters an existing product category, it tries to address where its rivals have gotten it wrong, especially when it comes to how users interact with the device. With the iPhone Duo, for instance, Apple used a “nano-texture” finish to minimize the crease and reflections found on other foldable phones, and it came up with a new interface to facilitate one-handed use on the outer screen. When speaking about the Apple Watch, former CEO Tim Cook told Fast Company that other smartwatch makers were “still using pinch-to-zoom and other gestures that we created for the iPhone,” instead of inventing new inputs like the Digital Crown. Going back to the original iPhone, Jobs bemoaned other smartphones’ reliance on physical control buttons, styluses, and keyboards, noting, “They’re not so smart and they’re not so easy to use.” Apple’s press release for the new MacBook doesn’t call out any such innovations, nor does it address the fatigue that comes from lifting your arm to poke a screen for extended periods. Its description of how the touchscreen works is in line with every touchscreen Windows laptop from the past decade-plus, noting that a tap on the screen is equivalent to clicking with your cursor. [Animation: Apple] From a marketing standpoint, the closest Apple comes to a rationale is the MacBook’s other big new feature: It’s the first Mac with an OLED screen, which Apple’s marketing video says looks “so real you’ll want to reach out and touch it.” But OLED isn’t a new laptop technology either, nor does it inherently solve the “ gorilla arm ” problem of extended touchscreen use. Speaking to Steven Levy of Wired , Apple executives provided a bit more of an explanation: Consumers are expecting touchscreens after years of using iPhones and iPads, and the folks at Apple felt the time was right, as the company didn’t have to compromise on things like weight and thickness. “There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing. Apple is at least making a few extra affordances for the new touchscreen. As The Verge points out , tapping the screen will cause certain elements to magnify, such as MacOS’s “traffic light” window controls and drop-down menus. Apple’s also updating its system gesture APIs so app makers can accommodate things like pinching, twisting, and multitouch. The iPhone’s “Dynamic Island” will appear on the new MacBook as well, providing a familiar touchpoint for iOS users. Still, Apple’s not reinventing MacOS around touch controls, nor is it deviating from a traditional clamshell design. Cook’s oft-repeated quote about the perils of converging a toaster and refrigerator —a dig at merging tablets and laptops into a single form—still sort-of holds up; Apple’s only trying to do that with the iPad . None of this means that touchscreen Macs are an unwelcome idea. While I rarely use the touchscreens on Windows laptops, they’re occasionally helpful for thumbing through articles, signing documents, and quickly tapping through a row of checkboxes. articles.title: Pentagon Models Forty-Seven Billion Dollar Cost for Prolonged Iranian Conflict
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox US President Donald Trump has held out on the possibility of restarting military operations after the Nov 3 midterm elections. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Oct 28, 2026, 09:05 AM Updated Oct 28, 2026, 10:09 AM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise The US military has spent over US$47 billion on the Iran war, Reuters said, more than 25% above the Pentagon’s July estimate of US$37.5 billion. The war has hurt Republican support before the Nov 3 election, as higher energy costs and falling approval ratings add political pressure on President Donald Trump. The Pentagon expects more than US$29 billion to replace munitions and over US$6 billion for lost equipment, while US officials say heavy fighting could restart after the midterms. AI generated WASHINGTON – The US military has spent over US$47 billion ( S$60.25 billion ) so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defence Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly. The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the Nov 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years. The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt US President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than US$29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict. More than US$6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “platform losses”, which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war. Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February , predicting that the conflict would last a short time. Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defences so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs (joint direct attack munitions), which are plentiful. But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defences, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible. Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections . US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so. The latest Pentagon estimate compares with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s July estimate of US$37.5 billion for the cost of the war. While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks. articles.title: New Delhi Election Takedowns Expose Platforms Subservience to Indian Censorship
articles.content: Instagram restored a reel posted by legal news outlet LiveLaw after restricting access to it for users in India . The reel explained the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) position in an affidavit before the Supreme Court . Instagram’s notice said: “We received a legal request to restrict this content.” The restriction affected an explainer about a public court filing in proceedings concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. LiveLaw said that the video contained no critical commentary and that the same video remained available on YouTube . What did Instagram disclose? LiveLaw reported that Instagram had not explained which law the reel allegedly violated or disclosed the nature of the request. The notice names no requester, legal provision, order or reference number . LiveLaw’s report was updated on October 27, 2026, to state that Instagram had restored the reel . The report does not say whether the platform explained its decision to restore the video or provided further details about the original request. Which legal route was used? India has separate legal routes that can lead to content being restricted online. Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides for government directions to block public access to information on specified grounds. The Blocking Rules, 2009 set out the related procedure . Section 79(3)(b) of the Act addresses intermediary liability when a platform fails to act after receiving notice from the government or its agencies that information is unlawful. MediaNama has reported that the Sahyog Portal routes requests under this provision. Instagram’s notice cites neither provision . The available material therefore does not establish which legal route, if any, led to the restriction. articles.content: Subscribed with another email? Logout and Login with that one. Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription Updated - October 28, 2026 11:19 am IST - NEW DELHI Security personnel detaining a student activist during a protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi. | Photo Credit: FILE PHOTO The cases have been registered under various charges, including violation of prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), vandalism and obstruction of public servants, among others. While the accused have not yet been named in these FIRs, the police are working to identify the protesters and those who “mobilised” them, officials said. Police teams are examining CCTV footage as part of the investigations, and action will be initiated against those identified, officials said. The FIRs were registered as protests continued over several days following a call by various youth outfits, including the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), on October 10, demanding the rollback of the SIR and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Demonstrations by student groups, youth organisations and women’s organisations followed, along with a rally by the INDIA bloc on October 12. Officials said the police had been detaining protesters and registering cases on a daily basis for alleged violations during the demonstrations. Timely registration of FIRs was necessary to document the alleged offences and avoid delays that could be difficult to justify during court proceedings. The police have also registered an FIR and arrested four occupants of a car allegedly seen carrying wooden sticks and batons near Connaught Place on October 11. The Uttar Pradesh-registered vehicle has been seized and remains in police custody. The car triggered controversy after it was spotted near the protest site with a large number of wooden sticks inside. Journalists and protesters raised concerns about the vehicle, but police personnel initially allowed it to leave the area. The occupants were later seen near the demonstrations brandishing sticks and confronting protesters. After videos of the incident circulated widely on social media, the Deputy Commissioner of Police (New Delhi) said on X that the vehicle had been taken to a police station for verification and that a search had found “nothing illegal or objectionable”. The occupants were also found to have no criminal records, the police had said. However, the police have now registered an FIR and arrested the four occupants. Investigators said they are also identifying other people associated with the accused and involved in violence during the protests. Separately, the Delhi Police have registered at least 10 FIRs after taking cognisance of social media posts alleging that right-wing activists assaulted protesters during the anti-SIR demonstrations. Investigations into those cases are under way. Officials said the police had not received a call on the emergency helpline 112 regarding the alleged attacks on protesters. The police are also examining videos circulating on social media that purportedly show a vehicle carrying several khaki uniforms, along with footage of alleged assaults on demonstrators, to identify those involved and investigate the incidents.
